title: Heat in the Environment
seo_title: Grade 7 Science: Heat in the Environment Worksheets (Ontario Curriculum)
standard_text: Describe how heat moves in the environment, including the greenhouse effect and convection in air and water; assess the effects of climate change and human uses of heat; evaluate ways to conserve energy. (summary of the Ontario Science and Technology curriculum, 2022, Strand E: Earth and Space Systems – Heat in the Environment)
meta_desc: Free Grade 7 science worksheets on the greenhouse effect, climate change, heat sources, heat pumps and saving energy. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Burning fossil fuels adds CO₂ and warms the climate; insulation and renewable heat save energy.
body_html:
How to think about it

The Sun heats Earth unevenly, which drives winds and ocean currents.

  • Greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide trap heat; more of them make the climate warmer.
  • Signs in Ontario: shorter ice seasons, warmer winters, more extreme weather.
  • Insulation, heat pumps, solar heating, trees and sealing drafts reduce energy use.
Example

Which gas from cars traps heat?

burning gasoline makes it

Answer: carbon dioxide

Example

Why are cities hotter than farmland?

asphalt absorbs heat

fewer trees

Answer: urban heat island

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up weather and climate.
  • Thinking the greenhouse effect is only bad (it keeps Earth livable).
  • Thinking the ozone hole causes global warming.

faq.a: Gases in the air trap some of the heat radiated from Earth, keeping the planet warm.

faq.q: How is climate change affecting Ontario?
faq.a: Winters are warmer, lakes freeze later, and heat waves and heavy storms are more common.

faq.q: How can we reduce heat loss from homes?
faq.a: Add insulation, seal drafts, use efficient windows and heat pumps, and lower the thermostat.

items.q: Nathan's class wants to reduce greenhouse gases. Which action would help?
items.e: This reduces greenhouse gases or removes CO₂ from the air.

items.q: How can planting trees help keep a house cool?
c: Trees shade the house and release water vapour that cools the air.
items.e: Shade reduces air-conditioning use.

items.q: Maya graphed carbon dioxide (CO₂) measured at Mauna Loa, Hawaii. What trend does it show?
c: CO₂ went up and down randomly.
CO₂ in the air has been decreasing.
CO₂ in the air has been increasing.
items.e: Each later year has a higher value.

items.q: How does a heat pump warm a house?
c: It moves heat from the outside air or ground into the house.
items.e: Heat pumps are efficient.

items.q: About what percentage of the air is oxygen?
items.e: Roughly one-fifth.

items.q: Which action reduces the energy used to heat a home?
c: sealing drafts around windows and doors
turning the heat to the highest setting
items.e: Weatherstripping keeps heat in.

items.q: Priya's class wants to reduce greenhouse gases. Which action would help?
c: cycling or walking for short trips
items.e: This reduces greenhouse gases or removes CO₂ from the air.

items.q: Olivia's class is studying causes of global warming. How does burning coal in power plants contribute?
c: It adds carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas, to the air.
It makes Earth closer to the sun.
It makes a hole in the ozone layer that lets in heat.
It does not affect the air.
items.e: Greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere.

items.q: Kai asks what is mainly causing the rise shown in the graph. What is the best answer?
c: more sunlight from a closer sun
people burning fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas
items.e: Burning fossil fuels releases CO₂ that was stored underground for millions of years.

items.q: Which is a renewable source of heat?
items.e: Solar energy will not run out.

items.q: Olivia's class wants to reduce greenhouse gases. Which action would help?
c: using solar and wind energy instead of coal
items.e: This reduces greenhouse gases or removes CO₂ from the air.

items.q: Benjamin's class is studying causes of global warming. How does driving gasoline cars contribute?
c: It makes Earth closer to the sun.
It does not affect the air.
It adds carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas, to the air.
It makes a hole in the ozone layer that lets in heat.
items.e: Greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere.

items.q: What is thermal pollution?
c: warm water released into rivers or lakes that harms aquatic life
items.e: Warm water holds less oxygen.

items.q: Which gas is the second most common in the air?
items.e: About 21%.

items.q: Which gas from burning fossil fuels adds most to the greenhouse effect?
items.e: More CO₂ traps more heat.

items.q: Which heat source comes from inside Earth?
items.e: Ground-source heat pumps use it.

items.q: Using Emma's graph, how much did CO₂ increase from 1960 to 2020?
Which gas makes up most of the air?
items.e: About 78%.

items.q: In the carbon cycle, what does cutting down and burning forests do?
c: adds carbon dioxide to the air
removes carbon dioxide from the air
has no effect on carbon dioxide
items.e: Photosynthesis and oceans remove it; respiration, decay and combustion add it.

items.q: Ava is collecting evidence that Earth's climate is warming. Which is the strongest scientific evidence?
c: It was cold in my town last Tuesday.
Arctic sea ice in summer covers less area than it did 40 years ago.
A movie showed a big storm.
My friend says winters used to be colder.
items.e: Strong evidence comes from many measurements over many years, not one day or one opinion.

items.q: Which is a sign of climate change in Ontario?
c: the Sun rising in the west
lakes freezing later and thawing earlier than in the past
items.e: Ice-cover data shows the change.

gases in the atmosphere trap heat and keep Earth warm
items.e: Without it, Earth would be frozen.

items.q: Ethan is collecting evidence that Earth's climate is warming. Which is the strongest scientific evidence?
c: My friend says winters used to be colder.
Spring comes earlier and many plants bloom sooner.
One summer day was very hot.
A movie showed a big storm.
items.e: Strong evidence comes from many measurements over many years, not one day or one opinion.

items.q: In the carbon cycle, what does volcanoes erupting do?
c: has no effect on carbon dioxide
adds carbon dioxide to the air
removes carbon dioxide from the air
items.e: Photosynthesis and oceans remove it; respiration, decay and combustion add it.

items.q: What is climate change?
c: long-term changes in Earth's temperatures and weather patterns
the change from day to night
items.e: Weather is day to day; climate is over many years.

items.q: Why is permafrost thawing in northern Canada a problem?
c: Buildings and roads sink, and stored greenhouse gases are released.
items.e: Warming changes northern landscapes.

items.q: Why do ocean currents and winds move heat around the planet?
c: Uneven heating makes warm fluids rise and cool fluids sink, causing currents.
items.e: Convection on a planet-wide scale.

items.q: Emma is collecting evidence that Earth's climate is warming. Which is the strongest scientific evidence?
c: Air bubbles in ice cores show CO₂ is much higher now than in the past 800 000 years.
One summer day was very hot.
It was cold in my town last Tuesday.
A movie showed a big storm.
items.e: Strong evidence comes from many measurements over many years, not one day or one opinion.

items.q: Mei is collecting evidence that Earth's climate is warming. Which is the strongest scientific evidence?
c: It was cold in my town last Tuesday.
A movie showed a big storm.
One summer day was very hot.
Mountain glaciers around the world are shrinking.
items.e: Strong evidence comes from many measurements over many years, not one day or one opinion.

items.q: Hana is collecting evidence that Earth's climate is warming. Which is the strongest scientific evidence?
c: Thermometer records show the average global temperature has risen about 1 °C since the late 1800s.
It was cold in my town last Tuesday.
One summer day was very hot.
A movie showed a big storm.
items.e: Strong evidence comes from many measurements over many years, not one day or one opinion.

items.q: Which gases are greenhouse gases?
c: carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour
items.e: These gases absorb heat.

items.q: What is mainly made when natural gas (methane) burns completely?
items.e: Fossil fuels contain carbon (and hydrogen).

items.q: Why are fossil fuels described as non-renewable?
c: They are made from sunlight daily.
They can be regrown each year.
They take millions of years to form, so they will run out.
items.e: Finite.

items.q: What is mainly made when diesel burns completely?
items.e: Fossil fuels contain carbon (and hydrogen).

items.q: Which greenhouse gas is mainly released by rotting garbage in landfill sites?
items.e: Carbon dioxide from burning; methane from cattle, rice and landfill.

items.q: Why is sea level rising?
c: Melting land ice adds water, and warmer water expands.
items.e: Both effects raise the ocean.

items.q: Why do Indigenous communities' traditional homes, like the longhouse or igloo, suit their climates?
c: They have no relation to climate.
They use local materials that hold or block heat to keep people comfortable.
They were all made of metal.
They were built only for looks.
items.e: Snow is a good insulator in an igloo.

items.q: Does global warming mean every day will be hotter?
c: No. It means the long-term average is rising; there are still cold days.
It means it never snows again.
items.e: Climate is the long-term pattern.

items.q: Which greenhouse gas is mainly released by burning gasoline in cars?
items.e: Carbon dioxide from burning; methane from cattle, rice and landfill.

items.q: Which greenhouse gas is mainly released by burning forests to clear land?
items.e: Carbon dioxide from burning; methane from cattle, rice and landfill.

items.q: What is the greenhouse effect?
c: The sun gets closer in summer.
The ozone layer lets heat in.
Gases in the atmosphere trap some of Earth's heat, keeping the planet warm enough for life.
items.e: Without it, Earth would be far colder. More greenhouse gases trap more heat.

items.q: Which greenhouse gas is mainly released by rice paddy fields?
items.e: Carbon dioxide from burning; methane from cattle, rice and landfill.

items.q: Which greenhouse gas is mainly released by coal-fired power plants?
items.e: Carbon dioxide from burning; methane from cattle, rice and landfill.

items.q: How do forests help reduce carbon dioxide in the air?
c: Trees make carbon dioxide all day.
Trees take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis.
items.e: Cutting forests removes this help.

items.q: Is the greenhouse effect always harmful?
c: No. A natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth livable; extra greenhouse gases cause extra warming.
items.e: The problem is the increase.

items.q: Which greenhouse gas is mainly released by leaks from natural gas pipes?
items.e: Carbon dioxide from burning; methane from cattle, rice and landfill.

items.q: What human activity adds the most carbon dioxide to the air?
items.e: Coal, oil and gas release CO₂ when burned.

items.q: What is mainly made when coal burns completely?
items.e: Fossil fuels contain carbon (and hydrogen).

items.q: Why are coal, oil and gas called fossil fuels?
c: They formed from the remains of living things millions of years ago.
They come from rocks in the core.
items.e: Stored carbon.

items.q: Which greenhouse gas is mainly released by cattle digesting grass?
items.e: Carbon dioxide from burning; methane from cattle, rice and landfill.

items.q: Why does a metal bench feel colder than a wooden one on the same day?
c: Metal conducts energy away from your hand faster.
Wood is warmer than the air.
items.e: Both are the same temperature.

items.q: Why is rubber used for the soles of shoes for walking on a hot road?
c: It is a good conductor of heat, so heat flows through it quickly.
It is a poor conductor of heat, so the feet do not get burnt.
It is the most colourful material.
items.e: Choose a material by how well it conducts heat.

items.q: Which material is best for the handle of a frying pan?
items.e: It is a poor conductor of heat, so the handle does not get too hot to hold.

items.q: Two pots of water get the same amount of heat. Pot A has 1 kg and pot B has 2 kg. Which warms up more?
items.e: Less mass means a bigger temperature change.

items.q: Olivia's teacher asks for an example of conduction. Which is the best example?
c: warm air rising above a campfire
a pan heating up on a stove burner
an oven fan moving hot air around food
a hair dryer blowing hot air
items.e: Energy moves between objects that are touching.

items.q: Why can radiation travel through space but conduction cannot?
c: Radiation is a wave and needs no particles; conduction needs particles.
items.e: Infrared.

items.q: What is thermal energy?
c: the total kinetic energy of all the particles in an object
items.e: More particles at the same temperature means more thermal energy.

items.q: Why is thick cloth used for oven gloves?
c: It is the most colourful material.
It is a good conductor of heat, so heat flows through it quickly.
It is a poor conductor of heat and protects the hands from hot trays.
items.e: Choose a material by how well it conducts heat.

items.q: Why does sand on a beach get hot faster than the ocean water?
c: Sand changes temperature more easily than water with the same energy.
items.e: Different materials change temperature differently.

items.q: Noah's teacher asks for an example of convection. Which is the best example?
c: sunlight warming Earth through empty space
a pan heating up on a stove burner
warm air rising from a heater and spreading through a room
items.e: Energy is carried by a moving liquid or gas.

items.q: Kai's teacher asks for an example of radiation. Which is the best example?
c: a hair dryer blowing hot air
a sea breeze blowing toward land on a sunny day
a pan heating up on a stove burner
items.e: Energy travels as light or infrared waves, even through empty space.

items.q: Why is a paper cup with a cardboard sleeve used for a cup for hot coffee to take away?
c: It is the most colourful material.
It is a good conductor of heat, so heat flows through it quickly.
The sleeve is a poor conductor of heat, so it protects your hand.
items.e: Choose a material by how well it conducts heat.

items.q: In which direction is energy transferred when two objects touch?
c: from the hotter object to the cooler one
from the cooler object to the hotter one
items.e: Until they reach the same temperature.

items.q: Ethan's teacher asks for an example of conduction. Which is the best example?
c: feeling the heat from a campfire while sitting a few feet away
a heat lamp keeping food warm
a metal spoon getting hot in a pot of soup
items.e: Energy moves between objects that are touching.

items.q: What tool do you need to measure a change in temperature?
items.e: Measure before and after.

items.q: What is the difference between temperature and thermal energy?
c: Temperature measures how hot something is; thermal energy also depends on how much material there is.
items.e: A bath at 40 °C has more thermal energy than a cup at 90 °C.

items.q: What is thermal equilibrium?
c: when objects reach the same temperature and there is no net energy transfer
items.e: No more change.

items.q: What does temperature measure?
c: the average kinetic energy (motion) of the particles
the total energy of all the particles
items.e: Faster particles mean higher temperature.

items.q: Energy is transferred from a hot stove to a pot of water. What happens to the stove's particles near the pot?
items.e: Energy moves from hotter to cooler.

items.q: When you heat water, what happens to its particles?
items.e: Adding energy increases kinetic energy.

items.q: A town switches its power plant from coal to wind. What should happen to its CO₂ emissions?
items.e: Wind turbines do not burn fuel.

items.q: How did the Earth's early atmosphere get its oxygen?
c: Algae and plants made it by photosynthesis.
items.e: Over billions of years.

items.q: Ava wants to test whether the type of material affects temperature change. Which setup is best?
c: different masses of each under different lamps
sand in sun and water in shade
the same mass of sand, water and soil under the same lamp for the same time
items.e: Keep everything the same except the material.

items.q: How can people reduce their carbon dioxide emissions?
c: use less energy, travel by bike or public transport, and use renewable electricity
items.e: Many small changes.

items.q: Noah adds 100 g of 80 °C water to 100 g of 20 °C water. About what temperature is the mixture?
items.e: Equal masses meet in the middle: (80 + 20) ÷ 2 = 50 °C.

items.q: Why do scientists study air bubbles trapped in ancient ice?
c: They show how much carbon dioxide was in the air long ago.
They show the age of the Moon.
items.e: Ice cores.

c: Less mass needs less energy to reach the same temperature.
The small pan got more heat.
items.e: Mass affects temperature change.

items.q: Emma hears a claim that global warming is caused by the hole in the ozone layer. Is this correct?
c: No. The ozone hole and global warming are different problems.
Yes, the hole lets in heat.
items.e: Global warming is mainly caused by greenhouse gases.

items.q: Zoe adds 100 g of 80 °C water to 300 g of 20 °C water. Will the mixture be closer to 80 °C or 20 °C?
items.e: There is more cold water, so the final temperature is closer to 20 °C.

items.q: Ava wants to model the greenhouse effect. She puts thermometers in two jars in the sun, one covered with plastic wrap. Which will get warmer?
items.e: The cover traps heat, like greenhouse gases.

items.q: Why is methane from cattle farming a concern?
c: Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas.
items.e: Agriculture.

c: The ocean makes its own heat.
Large amounts of water change temperature slowly.
items.e: Water keeps nearby land from getting very hot or very cold.

items.q: Ethan reads that ice cores show CO₂ and temperature rose and fell together in the past. What does this suggest?
c: CO₂ has no effect on climate.
items.e: The pattern supports the link.

items.q: What is a carbon footprint?
c: the size of a person's shoe
the amount of greenhouse gas released by a person's activities
items.e: Can be reduced.

items.q: Why is it hard to stop climate change quickly?
c: Carbon dioxide stays in the air for a long time and the world uses lots of fossil fuels.
Carbon dioxide disappears in a day.
items.e: Global problem.

items.q: Why do scientists use temperature records from thousands of places around the world?
c: to find the global average, not just local weather
items.e: Global trends need global data.

items.q: How do trees help to slow climate change?
c: They take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis and store the carbon.
They give out carbon dioxide only.
items.e: Carbon store.
